title: Hernando de Soto's Expedition through the Southeast
intro: Hernando de Soto, a conquistador who had taken part in the conquest of the Inca Empire, led over 620 men and some 220 horses into La Florida, searching for gold and for a passage to China or the Pacific. The expedition ranged through what is now the south-eastern United States.
ending: At the fortified town of Mabila in 1540 the Spaniards, who had taken the paramount chief Tuskaloosa hostage, burned the town in nine hours of fighting: about 200 Spaniards died, according to Elvas, and an estimated 2,000 to 6,000 Native Americans. De Soto died of a fever on 21 May 1542, and Luis de Moscoso Alvarado took command. Of the recorded 700 participants at the start, between 300 and 350 survived; the expedition had found no gold and founded no colonies.

stops.text: De Soto landed nine ships with over 620 men and 220 horses in an area generally identified as south Tampa Bay, though Robert S. Weddle suggested Charlotte Harbor or San Carlos Bay. He named the land Espíritu Santo.
stops.quote: In May 1539, de Soto landed nine ships with over 620 men and 220 horses in an area of La Florida generally identified as the current location of south Tampa Bay.

stops.text: The army seized stored food, took women as slaves for the soldiers' sexual gratification and forced men and boys to serve as bearers. De Soto struck first at Chief Vitachuco's people and thousands were killed; 900 survivors took refuge in Two-mile Pond.
stops.quote: 900 survivors took refuge in the pond, specifically Two-mile Pond in Melrose, where they continued to fight, while swimming.

stops.text: The expedition spent its first winter at Anhaica, the capital of the Apalachee people, just east of today's Tallahassee. It is one of the few places on the route where archaeologists have found physical traces of the expedition.
stops.quote: De Soto's first winter encampment was at Anhaica, the capital of the Apalachee people. It is one of the few places on the route where archaeologists have found physical traces of the expedition.

stops.text: Hearing of gold mined toward the sun's rising, the expedition turned north-east through Georgia. Researchers believe, from glass trade beads and metal objects found near the Ocmulgee River in 2009, that it stopped in Telfair County.
stops.quote: Based on archaeological finds made in 2009 at a remote, privately owned site near the Ocmulgee River, researchers believe that de Soto's expedition stopped in Telfair County.

stops.text: Fearing that word of the losses would reach Spain if his men reached the ships at Mobile Bay, de Soto led them away from the Gulf coast into inland Mississippi, most likely near Tupelo, where they spent the winter. The route beyond Mabila is contested.
stops.quote: He moved into inland Mississippi, most likely near present-day Tupelo, where they spent the winter.

legs.title: West of the Mississippi and de Soto's death

stops.text: Having crossed Arkansas, the expedition went as far inland as the Caddo River, where it clashed with the Tula, whom the Spaniards called the most skilled and dangerous warriors they had met. This may have happened near Caddo Gap.
stops.quote: The expedition went as far inland as the Caddo River, where they clashed with a Native American tribe called the Tula in October 1541.

stops.text: De Soto died of a fever in the village of Guachoya; sources disagree whether it lay near Lake Village, Arkansas, or Ferriday, Louisiana. His men hid his death, and according to one source sank his body in the Mississippi.
stops.quote: De Soto died of a fever on 21 May 1542, in the native village of Guachoya.

stops.text: After building seven pinnaces on the Mississippi, the survivors set off in July and drifted downriver under attack by war canoes led by the paramount chief Quigualtam; about 11 Spaniards were killed. They kept to the Gulf shore and after about 50 days reached the frontier town of Pánuco.
stops.quote: After about 50 days, they made it to the Pánuco River and the Spanish frontier town of Pánuco.

stops.text: After a month's rest at Pánuco the survivors reached Mexico City. Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza offered to lead another expedition to La Florida, but few survivors volunteered. Most stayed in the New World.
stops.quote: But, after they reached Mexico City and the Viceroy Don Antonio de Mendoza offered to lead another expedition to La Florida, few of the survivors volunteered.

notes: Years 1543 for Pánuco and Mexico City are inferred (the article gives none after 1542; 'By July' follows the winter after de Soto's death). Napituca and the Napituca Massacre (200 executed) are left out as a stop: the article gives no place for it; Melrose is the only place named for the Vitachuco battle, and its figures ('thousands') are the article's. Havana left out: no date for the departure. Coosa, Appalachian Mountains, eastern Tennessee, Autiamique and the Chickasaw attack: regions or places the article cannot locate. Telfair County is a county, kept because the article names it; Sunflower Landing wp title unverified; Guachoya's location disputed (Lake Village or Ferriday); the site's exact crossing and route beyond Mabila are contested. Mabila: article does not say the date; year from section heading 1540. Diseases (article says possibly carried, disputed) not given a stop.
